title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 18
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Building That Asks Nothing
passages.text:
A. Libraries are ancient; public libraries are not. Collections attached to temples, courts and universities existed for millennia, and access to them was controlled by membership of the institution that held them. A collection funded from taxation, open to any resident without payment, and lending material to be taken away is a nineteenth-century arrangement, and it was argued over at length before it was adopted anywhere.

B. Opposition came from two directions that rarely appear in the commemorative accounts. Ratepayers objected to funding a service they would not use, an argument that has never gone away. More interestingly, some booksellers and publishers opposed lending on the grounds that a borrowed book was a book unsold — a prediction that proved almost exactly backwards, since library provision expanded the reading population and the market along with it.

C. The reading room mattered as much as the collection and for reasons unconnected with books. Housing in industrial cities was crowded, cold and badly lit; a warm, quiet, lit room that could be entered without payment or explanation was a scarce commodity in itself. Attendance figures from the period track weather and fuel prices closely, which tells you what a substantial fraction of visitors were principally there for.

D. The service's defining characteristic is that it asks nothing of the person entering. There is no purchase, no appointment, no stated purpose and no assessment of need, and this is unusual to the point of being nearly unique among publicly funded services. It is also what makes the library difficult to evaluate: a service that does not record why people come cannot easily demonstrate what it achieved for them.

E. That evaluation problem has become the central threat. Lending figures have fallen in most high-income countries while visits have not fallen proportionally, because the building is now used for things the statistics were never designed to count — internet access, form-filling, study space, warmth, childcare of an informal kind, and simply being somewhere without spending. A measure built around borrowing registers all of this as decline.

F. Where closures have been evaluated afterwards, the results have been consistent enough to be worth stating. Use does not transfer to the next nearest branch in anything like full measure; a substantial proportion of use simply stops, and the loss falls hardest on those least able to travel or to substitute a paid alternative. The saving is real and immediate; the cost is real, delayed, and distributed among people who were not consulted.

passages.title: Mostly Not Taste
passages.text:
What people call taste is mostly smell. The tongue detects a small number of qualities — sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury — and everything that distinguishes a strawberry from a raspberry, or coffee from burnt toast, arrives through the nose, largely from the back of the mouth as air passes upward during chewing and swallowing. This is why food becomes unrecognisable during a heavy cold, and why the loss is described by sufferers as a loss of taste when it is nothing of the kind.

The distribution of receptors has been misrepresented for over a century. The familiar diagram assigning sweetness to the tip of the tongue and bitterness to the back derives from a misreading of an early study that reported small differences in threshold, not exclusive regions. All qualities are detectable across the tongue. The diagram survives in textbooks and on packaging long after the science stopped supporting it, which is a useful illustration of how a memorable image outlives its evidence.

Bitterness is the quality with the clearest evolutionary story and the most variation between people. A large family of receptors detects bitter compounds, many of which are toxic in plants, and sensitivity to specific compounds varies enormously between individuals for genetic reasons. A vegetable that is pleasantly sharp to one person is genuinely, physically unpleasant to another, which makes a certain amount of childhood food refusal a matter of perception rather than behaviour.

Texture and temperature modify perception more than most people credit. The same liquid tastes markedly sweeter warm than cold, which is why a soft drink at room temperature seems cloying; thickening a solution reduces perceived flavour intensity, which is a persistent difficulty in reformulating foods for lower sugar or salt. These interactions mean that removing an ingredient rarely produces a food that tastes like the original with less of it.

Expectation is not a minor factor layered on top of sensation but part of the sensation itself. Colouring a drink to suggest a different fruit changes what people report tasting; price information changes reported enjoyment and also the measured brain response; a description on a menu shifts perception of the dish it names. These are not errors of judgement corrected on closer attention — the experience itself differs, which is why blind testing produces results that surprise the people being tested.

The practical consequence concerns public health as much as cooking. Reducing salt or sugar abruptly produces rejection, but reducing it gradually across a category, over years, is largely unnoticed because preference adjusts to what is habitually eaten. Programmes built on that observation have achieved reductions that no amount of labelling or exhortation achieved, by changing the food rather than attempting to change the eater.

passages.title: The Arithmetic of the Bin
passages.text:
Recycling is unusual among environmental measures in that public enthusiasm for it substantially exceeds its measured benefit, while measures with far larger effects attract far less. The enthusiasm is not misplaced so much as misallocated, and understanding why requires separating materials that behave completely differently once collected.

Metals are the clear case. Aluminium recovered and remelted requires a small fraction of the energy needed to produce it from ore, the resulting metal is indistinguishable from new, and the process can be repeated indefinitely. Steel behaves similarly. For these materials the economics work without subsidy, collection is worth paying for, and the environmental case is not seriously contested by anyone.

Paper and glass sit in the middle and depend heavily on distance. Both are recovered successfully, but both are heavy relative to their value, and transporting them any great distance to a processing facility consumes much of the benefit. Glass in particular is close to break-even where it must travel far, and the sensible policy therefore differs between a dense city with a local plant and a scattered rural population, which is a conclusion that fits national uniform schemes badly.

Plastics are where the account diverges sharply from public belief. The category comprises many incompatible polymers that must be separated to be useful, contamination degrades the result, and most recycled plastic is remade into something of lower value that cannot itself be recycled again — a delay rather than a loop. Collection rates reported as recycling have historically included material exported for processing whose fate was poorly documented, and the tightening of import rules by receiving countries exposed how much of the system depended on that route.

The ordering of the standard hierarchy is the part most often ignored. Reduction and reuse sit above recycling for good reason: not producing an item avoids its entire footprint, while recycling recovers a fraction of the material and none of the manufacturing energy already spent. A container reused thirty times displaces thirty containers; the same container recycled displaces a portion of one. Public attention and municipal budgets are nonetheless concentrated almost entirely on the third tier.

None of this argues for abandoning collection, and the argument is frequently misrepresented that way. It argues for honesty about where the benefit lies — substantial for metals, conditional for paper and glass, limited and often overstated for plastics — and for the recognition that a household sorting its waste diligently has done something worth doing and something considerably smaller than the attention given to it implies.
